hints: Think about what molecule genes are made from and whether a gene is the whole molecule or just a short length of it.
Link that DNA section to its job - what type of molecule is built using the information in the gene?
walkthrough:
Start With DNA, Not a Cell**
Think of DNA as a very long instruction book. A gene is not the whole book, it is one short sequence of nucleotides that carries instructions for one job.

Link Gene To Protein**
That job is to code for one polypeptide chain. During protein synthesis the nucleotide sequence determines the amino acid sequence, so you get full marks for stating both the structure (DNA sequence) and the function (codes for polypeptide).
Final answer: A gene is a sequence / length of DNA that codes for a polypeptide (protein).

hints: Recall the three groups that must surround the central carbon in every amino acid, and check which ones are already drawn in Fig. 2.1.
Focus on the two carbons shown - the left carbon is the central alpha-carbon and the right carbon belongs to the acid group, so what atoms must be added to each side?
walkthrough:
Remember The Amino Acid Blueprint**
Every amino acid has a central carbon joined to H, an R group, an amino group $-NH_2$ and a carboxyl group $-COOH$. In glycine the R group is just H, so the left carbon in Fig. 2.1 already shows $H$ on top and bottom.

Complete Both Ends**
Join $-NH_2$ to the left carbon to complete the amino end. Join the right carbon to both $=O$ and $-O-H$ to make a complete carboxylic acid $-COOH$. That gives the smallest amino acid, glycine.
Final answer: Add $-NH_2$ to the central (left) carbon and add $-COOH$ ($C=O$ and $C-O-H$) to the right carbon to give $H_2N-CH_2-COOH$.

hints: Remember starch is not a single molecule but a mixture of an unbranched and a branched alpha-glucose polymer.
walkthrough:
Name The Two Starch Polymers**
Starch grains contain unbranched amylose with only 1,4-glycosidic bonds and branched amylopectin with 1,4- and 1,6-glycosidic bonds. Both are polymers of alpha-glucose.
Final answer: Amylose and amylopectin.

hints: Sort the four substances first - which is a single sugar monomer, which is two sugars joined, which is many sugars, and which is a protein?
Recall that polysaccharide means many monosaccharides joined, while macromolecule means any very large molecule including proteins and polysaccharides.
Check maltose carefully - it is larger than glucose but is it large enough to count as a polysaccharide or a macromolecule?
walkthrough:
Classify By Size And Type**
Glucose is a single monomer so only monosaccharide. Maltose is a disaccharide of two glucoses, so neither polysaccharide nor monosaccharide nor macromolecule. Starch is many glucoses so both polysaccharide and macromolecule.

Place The Enzyme Correctly**
Maltase is a protein enzyme. Proteins are very large polymers of amino acids, so maltase is a macromolecule but not a carbohydrate at all, giving x for polysaccharide and monosaccharide and tick for macromolecule.

Fill Every Box**
Cambridge awards one mark for the glucose + starch rows together, one for maltase and one for maltose. A common mistake is to tick macromolecule for maltose - only very large molecules like proteins and polysaccharides count.
Final answer: glucose: polysaccharide x, monosaccharide tick, macromolecule x; maltase: x, x, tick; maltose: x, x, x; starch: tick, x, tick.

hints: Compare growing barley in fields for a season with growing microbes in a fermenter - which can be scaled up faster and harvested more easily?
walkthrough:
Think Like An Industrial Producer**
Barley needs land, time and harvest, while microbes divide rapidly in a fermenter all year. That means cheap, continuous, large-scale enzyme supply that is easy to extract and can include faster or more tolerant versions.
Final answer: Microorganisms can be cultured in large quantities to produce large amounts of enzyme / easier to extract / higher rate of reaction / active over a greater temperature range.

hints: Look at the rising part of the curve from $10^{\circ}C$ to about $48^{\circ}C$ - what does heating do to molecular movement and meeting between enzyme and substrate?
Find the peak value on Fig. 2.3 and state what this temperature represents in enzyme language.
Look at the steep fall after the peak to zero at about $66^{\circ}C$ - what permanent change to active site shape explains loss of activity?
walkthrough:
Explain The Rise**
From $10^{\circ}C$ to about $48^{\circ}C$ activity rises from near zero to $100$%. More heat means more kinetic energy, so enzyme and starch molecules move faster and collide successfully with the active site more often.

Name The Optimum**
The peak at about $47-49^{\circ}C$ is the optimum temperature where a maximum number of active sites are binding substrate and activity is highest.

Explain The Fall By Denaturation**
Above the optimum activity falls steeply to zero at about $66^{\circ}C$. Excess heat vibrates and breaks weak hydrogen bonds, so the active site loses its complementary shape and substrate no longer fits. This denaturation is irreversible.

Final answer: Rise to optimum: increased temperature increases kinetic energy so increased rate of successful collisions / enzyme-substrate complex formation; optimum about $48^{\circ}C$ for maximum activity; above optimum active site denatures / loses shape so activity falls, e.g. hydrogen bonds break.

hints: If the new amylase resists heat, will its peak stay at $48^{\circ}C$ or move left or right, and will the peak height change?
Think about where the falling part of the new curve must go relative to the old curve to show activity at temperatures where the barley enzyme is already zero.
walkthrough:
Shift The Optimum Right**
Heat-stable means it keeps its shape at higher temperatures, so maximum activity still reaches $100$% but at a temperature to the right of $48^{\circ}C$. Draw the same shape moved right.

Keep The Curve To The Right**
The whole curve, especially the denaturation fall, must lie to the right of the original. It should still fall to zero but only beyond $66^{\circ}C$, showing the enzyme is still active where the barley enzyme is denatured.

Final answer: Sketch a similar bell curve with peak still at $100$% but shifted to the right (higher optimum); falling part stays to the right of original and meets the x-axis at higher temperature / meets y-axis at $50$% or below.
